raw_response:
I've been working this land for fifty years now, so I'll tell you how I'm thinking about this season.

## My reasoning

My 20 mu splits into roughly 12 mu of wheat-maize rotation on my better loam ground, and 8 mu of cotton on the sandier patch to the west — that land has always grown cotton and I'm not going to change it now. At my age, I don't experiment without a reason. What works, works.

My son works in town, so for heavy jobs — cotton picking especially — I hire day laborers from the village. My wife and I still handle most of the routine work, but I'm not picking 8 mu of cotton by hand anymore.

**Wheat (12 mu):** I plant in mid-October, improved semi-dwarf variety. I target about 470 kg/mu — that's what I got last year and the year before. My nitrogen strategy is split: roughly 12 kg N/mu as base fertilizer with the seedbed (compound 15-15-15 plus some urea), then 8 kg N/mu topdressed at jointing in March when I can see how the crop is tillering. Phosphorus around 6 kg P₂O₅/mu, potassium 5 kg K₂O/mu — our soil has built up reasonable P and K from years of double cropping, no need to overdo it. I irrigate 3-4 times depending on winter rainfall: pre-winter, jointing, heading, and grain-fill if April-May is dry. Groundwater isn't cheap anymore, so I don't water unless the crop needs it.

**Maize (same 12 mu, after wheat):** Tight window — I plant within 3-4 days of wheat harvest in mid-June, direct-seed with a hired planter operator. Hybrid seed, about 16 kg N/mu split between base and tasseling topdress. One or two irrigations in the dry spell before tasseling. Main pest concern is corn borer — I spray once if I see damage.

**Cotton (8 mu):** Plant mid-to-late April after the last cold spell. About 13 kg N/mu split three ways: base, first square, and flowering. Cotton needs more pesticide than grain — aphids, bollworm, spider mites. I spray 4-5 times through the season. Yield around 260 kg/mu lint in a normal year. Biggest expense is picking labor — 3 picks from September through October.

I keep some cash in reserve. If there's a drought and I need extra irrigation, or a bollworm outbreak, I need to be able to respond without borrowing.
